correctness.rationale: The simplex-volume determinant identity follows by writing the centered columns in terms of the n columns of vertex differences; the resulting n-by-n Gram factor has eigenvalues 1 (multiplicity n−1) and 1/(n+1). Trace AM–GM and the equality Gram matrix give exactly the inscribed regular simplices in the unit ball. Independently checked the cap ellipsoid comparison: its quadratic transverse-radius surplus vanishes at z=1 and z=−t and has leading coefficient 1−a²/b²=−2(1−nt)/((n−1)(1+t)); it is strictly positive in the intervening open interval when t<1/n. The affine images of the apex and base rim are the north pole and the latitude −1/n, with transverse radius sqrt(1−1/n²), so a centered regular base yields an attaining regular simplex. Transforming the volume back gives the first formula, and all attaining vertices must be on the contact set, which forces the claimed apex/base equality geometry. At t=1/n, nonnegative shifted heights w_i have sum squared equal to their sum of squares by the regular simplex frame identity, forcing exactly one nonzero height shift. For larger caps that regular simplex remains feasible and the full-ball equality case is both necessary and sufficient. The finite checker was inspected, not executed.
residual_risks: This validates the solid unit-cap theorem and equality cases as mathematics, not a priority claim or an extension to general truncated bodies.

evidence: Theorem 6.1 covers all parallel slices −1≤alpha<beta≤1 of the ball and gives the unit-ball enclosing branch exactly for alpha beta≤−1/n. In the nonball case Lemma 6.3 restricts sphere contacts to the two end latitudes, and Lemma 6.4 (6.8) gives the center/axis relations.
Horváth–Lángi Corollary 1 gives the full-ball maximum-simplex shape. The later indexed outer-ellipsoid result credits Todd for the cap ellipsoid and its transition.
broader_coverage.reasoning: Set beta=1. For alpha>−1/n, write a_G and b_G for the axial and transverse inverse-square radii in Güler–Gürtuna. The top contact and (6.8) give (1−tau)²=1/a_G=n(tau−alpha)(1−tau), hence tau=(1+n alpha)/(n+1); the bottom contact gives b_G=(1−1/n²)/(1−alpha²). These are the exact frozen ellipsoid, with the same transition and contact geometry, not merely a qualitative bound.

evidence: The prior axes send the lower contact to (alpha−tau)/(1−tau)=−1/n and the top contact to 1. The prior ball bound is tight for the regular simplex on those layers.

At the transition, for a feasible regular simplex the heights have sum zero and sum of squares (n+1)/n. From z_i≥−1/n and sum (z_i+1/n)²=(sum(z_i+1/n))², all but one shifted height vanish. In larger caps that simplex stays feasible.
claim_vs_prior_implication.reasoning: The affine map gives the prior full-ball bound times its inverse determinant, already attained by the known apex-base candidate; the earlier endpoint contact statement forces every smaller-cap optimizer to be of this type. At the endpoint the standard regular frame forces the same geometry, and for larger caps the feasible inscribed regular simplices are exactly the equality cases of the ball bound. Thus the values, both equality branches and saturation all follow, even though no inspected predecessor phrases that combination as a separate cap-simplex theorem.

evidence: The public MathOverflow answers and comments recover Firsching's apex-regular-base lower bound and show O’Rourke raised the contact condition as a question, not a theorem.

The Resultary odd-dimensional symmetric slab uses related geometry but differs in feasible set and optimizer, and the one-sided John contact frame concerns an inscribed rather than containing ellipsoid.
Güler–Gürtuna §5, (5.1), includes the exact solid cap as B_(alpha,1) with alpha=1−h.
equivalent_formulations.reasoning: The direct lower-bound answer and the symmetric-slab/inner-ellipsoid neighbours do not cover the frozen theorem, but the outer-ellipsoid reformulation lands exactly in an earlier proved class and gives a matching affine-ball certificate.

originality.rationale: The direct MathOverflow answer is only a prior lower bound, but the finding is a routine exact corollary of the earlier slab enclosing-ellipsoid theorem of Güler–Gürtuna combined with the classical maximum-simplex theorem in a ball. The earlier ellipsoid theorem literally includes a one-sided cap and already gives the same ellipsoid, boundary transition, and contact layers. The specialization gives base contact latitude −1/n after normalization, exactly the latitude of a regular simplex opposite its top vertex, so the standard volume bound is attained with the frozen equality geometry. This is established prior implication, not a conclusion from an inaccessible paper or a search snippet.
residual_risks: Todd's original scope beyond the ellipsoid result was not read directly. The rejection relies on the accessible and independently verified primary slab theorem and ball-simplex result, not on that access gap.

value.rationale: The solid-cap optimization is a well-motivated question, and the frozen exposition is useful. But as an exact-invariant contribution the result is determined mechanically by the prior explicit slab ellipsoid and its end contacts, affine invariance of the ball-simplex bound, and the already computed lower-bound construction. The threshold equality is an elementary regular-frame consequence; no independent unknown invariant or new regime survives in the frozen finding as stated.
residual_risks: The assessment concerns the incremental research contribution, not the pedagogical utility or truth of the cap theorem.
